abstract: Significance Human leukocyte antigens (HLAs) present peptides to T cells, thereby allowing them to recognize pathogen-infected and cancer cells. Conventionally, it was thought that peptides bind to HLA molecules in a conserved N- to C-terminal orientation. Here, we demonstrate that peptides in HLA-DP can also bind in a reverse C- to N-terminal orientation and show recognition of such reverse peptides by virus-specific human T cells from the memory repertoire. We provide the molecular basis for reverse binding by a high-resolution HLA–peptide crystal structure. Our findings have impact on our basic understanding of how peptides bind to HLA molecules and expand the identification of novel peptides recognized by T cells, which will help improving treatment of viral infections and cancers.
methods:
Methods
Cell Lines and Primary Material.
K562 cells lacking HLA class I and class II surface expression were cultured in Iscove’s modified Dulbecco’s medium (IMDM) (Lonza, Switzerland) with 10% fetal bovine serum (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), 200 mM L-glutamine (Lonza), and 10,000 U/ml penicillin/streptomycin (Lonza). Cells were transduced with HLA-DP using the pLZRS vector encoding for HLA-DPA1-T2A-DPB1-IRES-ΔNGFR or HLA-DPA1-IRES-GFP and HLA-DPB1-IRES-ΔNGFR. Purity of HLA-DP–expressing cells was verified by flow cytometry. T cells isolated from healthy donors were cultured in T cell medium consisting of IMDM with 5% fetal bovine serum, 5% human serum, 200 mM L-glutamine, 10,000 U/ml penicillin/streptomycin, and IL-2 (Novartis, Switzerland) as indicated below. Human samples were deidentified prior to use and the study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Leiden University Medical Centre.
HLA-DP Immunoaffinity Chromatography and Mass Spectrometry.
HLA-DP immunoaffinity chromatography was performed as recently described (
5
). Briefly, Protein A Sepharose bead (GE Healthcare)–purified B7/21 antibody was used to generate a 2.5 mg/ml immunoaffinity column. Approximately 1 × 10
8
cells/ml were lysed 2 h at 4°C using 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8), 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, 0.5% Zwittergent
®
3–12 detergent (Merck, Germany), and complete™ protease inhibitor cocktail (Merck). After centrifugation (13,640 g, 30 min, 4°C), supernatant was precleared using CL4B beads (GE Healthcare) and transferred to the immunoaffinity column. Elution from bound peptide–HLA-DP complexes was performed with 10% acetic acid. Subsequently, size filtration through a 10-kDa membrane (Merck) and freeze-drying were carried out. Mass spectrometry was performed as described elsewhere (
5
).
Peptide Data Analysis.
Peptide motifs were aligned and clustered with the previously published algorithm MoDec using default settings (
7
), except for the K562 dataset where the peptide input length was set to nine amino acids since K562 lack HLA class I expression. HLA-DP peptide elution datasets from EBV-LCL and K562 transduced were published earlier (
5
,
23
) and reanalyzed with MoDec. Datasets for HLA-DR and HLA-DQ were obtained from studies published by others (
9
,
10
) and were analyzed with MoDec.
Isolation of CMV-Specific T Cell Clones.
PBMCs from CMV-seropositive healthy donors were stimulated with 1 µM peptide mix (dependent on the HLA type of the donor;
Fig. 2
A
) at a concentration of 2 × 10
7
cells/ml in T cell medium supplemented with 20 U/ml IL-2 for 20 h. Peptides were synthesized in-house by our peptide synthesis facility. Cells were harvested and stained with the following fluorochrome-labeled monoclonal antibodies: anti-human CD3 (UCHT1) Alexa Fluor 700, CD4 (RPA-T4) FITC, and CD137 (4B4-1) APC (all from BD Biosciences, Germany) and CD154 (TRAP-1) PE (Beckman Coulter, USA). After sorting with BD FACSAria™, T cells were plated and expanded in single cells in 384-well plates together with 35-Gy irradiated allogeneic PBMCs (25,000 per well) in T cell medium supplemented with 200 U/ml IL-2 and 0.8 µg/ml phytohemagglutinin (PHA; Thermo Fisher Scientific). Seven days later, T cells were restimulated with 50,000 irradiated allogeneic PBMCs per well. Between days 3 and 5 after restimulation, growing T cell clones were transferred into 96-well plates. Subsequently, T cells were tested for peptide recognition and endogenously processed antigen against K562 cells as described below. Clonality of the T cell clones was analyzed by staining the variable domain from the T cell receptor β-chain with the Beta Mark TCR Vbeta Repertoire Kit (Beckman Coulter).
IFN-γ ELISA.
T cell clones were tested for IFN-γ production 10–14 d after restimulation. About 2,000 T cell clones were incubated overnight with 10,000 target cells in 384-well plates in 60 µl T cell medium supplemented with 20 U/ml IL-2. K562 transduced with either HLA-DPA1*02:01/DPB1*01:01 (K562-HLA-DP1) or HLA-DPA1*02:02/DPB1*05:01 (K562-HLA-DP5) were loaded with peptide as indicated for 1 h at 37°C and washed before coincubation with T cells. To test recognition of endogenously processed antigen, K562-DP1 or K562-DP5 cells transduced with pp65, IE1, and pp50 were used as target cells. Technical replicates of supernatants were analyzed for IFN-γ secretion using the Human IFN-γ ELISA Set (Diaclone, France) according to manufacturer’s instructions.
Ten-Day T Cell Stimulation Assay.
PBMCs from healthy CMV-seropositive donors that express HLA-DPB1*01:01 and/or HLA-DPB1*05:01 were incubated (37°C + 5% CO
2
) with 1 µg/mL peptide in IMDM (Lonza) with 10% fetal bovine serum (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 200 mM L-glutamine (Lonza), and 10,000 U/ml penicillin/streptomycin (Lonza). Half of medium was refreshed daily, and after 10 d of culturing, the cells were restimulated with the same peptide. After 1-h incubation, 5 µg/mL Brefeldin A (Sigma-Aldrich) was added and incubated for an additional 15 h. The reaction was stopped by washing in PBS, followed by Zombie-red staining (BioLegend). After incubation for 20 min at room temperature (RT), cells were fixated and permeabilized using the eBioscience Foxp3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer Set (Invitrogen), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Cells were incubated for 30 min at RT with an antibody mix containing Brilliant Violet Staining Buffer Plus (BD Biosciences), CD3-PE-Texas Red (7D6; Invitrogen), CD8-APC-H7 (SK1; BD Biosciences), CD4-BV510 (SK3; BD Biosciences), IFNγ-BV711 (B27; BD Biosciences), and TNFα-BV421 (Mab11; BD Biosciences). After incubation, cells were washed and resuspended in PBS containing 400 mg albumin for measurement on a 3-laser Aurora (Cytek Biosciences). Data were analyzed using OMIQ (
https://www.omiq.ai/
).
HLA-DP1-CLIP Expression and Purification.
The gene encoding the GP67 signal sequence and extracellular domains of the HLA-DP1 α- and β-chains (HLA-DPA1*02:01 and HLA-DPB1*01:01) were cloned into the pZIP3 bidirectional baculovirus expression vector (
24
). A DNA sequence encoding the Strep-TagII CLIP sequence (Strep-TagII-CLIP: WSHPQFEKGAPVSKMRMATPLLMQA) was inserted upstream of the gene encoding the HLA-DPB1 extracellular domain, connected by a flexible Factor Xa (FXa) cleavable linker (FXa recognition sequence underlined; GSGGS
IEGR
GSGSG) at the N terminus of the HLA-DPB1 gene. The C terminus of the construct encoded a Fos/Jun leucine zipper for the α- and β-chains, respectively, with both connected via 3C protease cleavage sites (LEVLFQGP) in between. The C terminus of the β-chain encoded a BirA biotinylation recognition site (GLNDIFEAQKIEWHE), and a polyhistidine-tag for purification of the expressed protein via immobilized metal affinity chromatography (IMAC). The DP1-CLIP molecule was expressed in High Five insect cells (Trichoplusia ni BTI-TN-5B1-4 cells; Thermo Fisher Scientific) using the Bac-to-Bac baculovirus system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to generate recombinant virus for protein expression. The High Five insect cells were infected with recombinant virus and incubated for 72 h at 27°C in shaking cultures (120 RPM). Culture supernatant containing the protein was separated from cells by centrifugation, followed by concentration and diafiltration using a Cogent M1 tangential flow filtration apparatus (Merck) with proteins then purified using a combination of IMAC (Nickel Sepharose 6 Fast Flow; Cytiva), size exclusion (Superdex 200, 16/600; Cytiva), and anion exchange (HiTrap Q HP column; Cytiva) chromatography.
Peptide Loading of HLA-DP1.
A 17-mer pp65 peptide (denoted as peptide 2) was synthesized by GL Biochem (China). The integrity of the peptides was verified by reverse-phase HPLC and mass spectrometry. HLA-DP1 was digested with Factor Xa (New England BioLabs, MA, USA) in the presence of 2 mM CaCl
2
to cleave the covalently linked Strep-TagII-CLIP peptide (WSHPQFEKGAPVSKMRMATPLLMQAGSGGSIEGRGSGSG). The Strep-TagII-CLIP peptide in HLA-DP1 was exchanged with the pp65
142–158
peptide using a 20-fold molar excess of peptide to HLA-DP1 in a buffer comprising 50 mM trisodium citrate pH 5.4 and 5 mM EDTA at 37°C for 24–72 h in the presence of HLA-DM (1:5 molar ratio HLA-DM:HLA-DP1). Peptide 2–loaded HLA-DP1 was separated from unloaded HLA-DP1-Strep-TagII-CLIP using Strep-Tactin Sepharose (IBA, Gottingen, Germany). Peptide 2–HLA-DP1 was subjected to 3C protease cleavage in order to remove the Fos/Jun leucine zippers and further purified using anion exchange (HiTrap Q HP column; Cytiva) chromatography. Final purified proteins were pooled and concentrated to 10 mg/ml.
Crystallization, Data Collection, and Processing.
Crystallization of the peptide 2–HLA-DP1 complex was carried out using the broad screen sitting-drop vapor-diffusion method (Monash Molecular Crystallisation Facility, Monash University, Clayton, Australia). Crystal hits were obtained in solution containing 0.1 M sodium cacodylate pH 5.5 and 20 to 25% PEG4000. Crystals were cryoprotected in 20% glycerol prior to flash freezing in liquid N
2
. Data were collected at the microfocus beamline (MX2) of the Australian Synchrotron (Victoria, Australia) and autoprocessed using program XDS (
25
) at the Australian Synchrotron.
Structure Determination, Refinement, and Validation.
Complex structures were solved by molecular replacement in PHASER (
26
), CCP4 (
27
) suite using a separate search model of HLA-DP5 (PDB ID: 3WEX). Iterative rounds of model building in Coot and restrained refinement using REFMAC (CCP4 suite) (
27
) and PhenixRefine (PHENIX) (
28
) were carried out. The crystal structures were validated using the Protein Data Bank (PDB) structure validation server. Data processing and refinement statistics are summarized in
SI Appendix
, Table S1
. The Ramachandran statistic of final models revealed 99.5% of residues in favored regions, with no outlier residues. All structural figures were generated by PyMOL (
http://www.pymol.org/
).
Accession Number.
The X-ray crystal structure of peptide 2–HLA-DP1 was deposited in the PDB with the accession code 7T6I.

Cell Lines and Primary Material.
K562 cells lacking HLA class I and class II surface expression were cultured in Iscove’s modified Dulbecco’s medium (IMDM) (Lonza, Switzerland) with 10% fetal bovine serum (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), 200 mM L-glutamine (Lonza), and 10,000 U/ml penicillin/streptomycin (Lonza). Cells were transduced with HLA-DP using the pLZRS vector encoding for HLA-DPA1-T2A-DPB1-IRES-ΔNGFR or HLA-DPA1-IRES-GFP and HLA-DPB1-IRES-ΔNGFR. Purity of HLA-DP–expressing cells was verified by flow cytometry. T cells isolated from healthy donors were cultured in T cell medium consisting of IMDM with 5% fetal bovine serum, 5% human serum, 200 mM L-glutamine, 10,000 U/ml penicillin/streptomycin, and IL-2 (Novartis, Switzerland) as indicated below. Human samples were deidentified prior to use and the study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Leiden University Medical Centre.

body:
Human leukocyte antigens (HLAs) present peptides to T cells enabling them to recognize virus-infected or malignant cells. CD8
+
T cells recognize peptides presented in HLA class I, whereas CD4
+
T cells bind to HLA class II molecules. HLA class I molecules consist of two chains, an α-chain and an invariant subunit called β2-microglobulin (
1
). The α1- and α2-domains of the α-chain form the peptide-binding groove with closed ends. Due to the closed ends of the peptide-binding groove, HLA class I binding peptides are usually constrained in their length between 8 and 10 amino acids.
HLA class II molecules on the other hand consist of an α- and a β-chain, which form an open-ended peptide-binding groove, and peptides consisting of more than 12 amino acids bind to HLA class II (
2
). Specific amino acid residues from the peptide, called anchors, preferably bind into pockets (P) of the HLA molecule, influenced by charge and size of the amino acids and allotype-specific properties of the HLA molecule. The most important anchor residues of the peptide are at positions P1, P4, P6, and P9 of the HLA class II groove (
3
). The preferred amino acids binding to those pockets form the binding motif of an HLA allotype.
Conventionally, peptides are considered to bind in HLA class II P1–P9 from their N- to C-terminus (further referred as “forward”). Previous crystal structures revealed that class II–associated invariant chain peptide (CLIP) can also bind in a reverse orientation (C- to N-terminus, “reverse”) in HLA-DR (
4
). However, it has been unclear if reverse bound peptides are indeed naturally processed and presented in human cells, and more importantly, if T cells are able to recognize those peptides. This would be of considerable interest since it would substantially increase the repertoire of T cells targeting pathogenic or cancer antigens. In contrast, this phenomenon was not described in HLA class I molecules, which might be due to the closed ends of the peptide-binding groove.
In this study, we demonstrated in 9 out of 14 most frequent HLA-DP alleles reverse binding motifs by peptide elution and mass spectrometry. We further identified two peptides in proteins of the widespread cytomegalovirus (CMV) with a reverse motif restricted to HLA-DP1 (HLA-DPB1*01:01/HLA-DPA1*02:01) and HLA-DP5 (DPA1*02:02/DPB1*05:01). These two reverse peptides are efficiently recognized by high-avidity human CD4
+
T cells from the memory repertoire of CMV-positive healthy donors at similar frequencies as forward peptides. Finally, we demonstrated reverse peptide binding by high-resolution structure. These findings change our fundamental understanding of peptide binding modes to HLA molecules and demonstrate how human T cell responses are broadened to pathogens and cancer cells.
Results
Reverse Peptide Motifs Are Found in Most Frequent HLA-DP Alleles.
We previously found first indications that a reverse peptide motif (proposed binding from the C- to N-terminus) exists in HLA-DP5 (
5
). Here, we investigated whether reverse motifs are also found in other HLA-DP molecules encoded by different alleles. K562 cells lacking endogenous HLA class I and class II expression were transduced with HLA-DPB1 and HLA-DPA1 genes. After confirming HLA-DP expression by flow cytometry and large-scale expansion of these transduced cell lines, peptides were measured by mass spectrometry after immunoaffinity chromatography and peptide elution (
5
,
6
). Using the recently published motif deconvolution algorithm (MoDec) to determine peptide core motifs (
7
), we found reverse motifs in 9 out of 14 analyzed HLA allotypes (
Fig. 1
A
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S1
). The frequencies of peptides clustering in the reverse motif were between 11 and 64%, with the highest frequency in HLA-DP5 (
Fig. 1
B
). Besides a lack of HLA expression, K562 cells do not express molecules involved in HLA class II peptide presentation like HLA-DM, HLA-DO, and the invariant chain. To investigate if reverse peptide motifs are similarly observed in cells expressing those molecules resembling more natural conditions, we reanalyzed our published HLA-DP peptide dataset from Epstein–Barr virus lymphoblastoid B-cell lines (EBV-LCL) (
5
) with MoDec, which was previously analyzed with Gibbs clustering (
8
). We found reverse motifs in the same HLA-DP allotypes as in HLA-DP–transduced K562 cells (
SI Appendix
, Table S1
). In addition, the frequencies of peptides clustering in the reversed motif were also within the same range of 10 to 63%.
Fig. 1.
Reverse motif is frequently found in HLA-DP alleles. (
A
) K562 cells were transduced with HLA-DPB1/DPA1 combinations as depicted, and high-confident HLA-DP peptides were used to determine the peptide core motif by MoDec. On the X-axis, the amino acid position within the core is shown, and the Y-axis refers to the relative frequency of the amino acid at this position. The frequency of peptides clustered in either forward or reverse motif is shown. Peptides that could not be categorized are in the “flat motif” cluster. (
B
) Overview of forward or reverse peptide motif frequency with different HLA-DPB1/DPA1 combinations.
We also analyzed with MoDec a small dataset from published HLA-DR and HLA-DQ allotypes (
9
,
10
) (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
). Here, we were not able to identify a reverse motif.
In conclusion, the observed reverse peptide motifs were frequently found across HLA-DP allotypes and not restricted to one cell type.
Identification of HLA-DP–Restricted CMV-Derived Peptides and Isolation of Reactive T Cell Clones.
Since reverse peptide motifs are based on a pattern of thousands of peptides but not on actual binding of individual peptides, we investigated whether peptides binding from the C- to N-terminus (further referred as “reverse peptides”) to HLA-DP naturally exist and can be recognized by human T cells.
To address this, we determined CMV-specific peptides presented in HLA-DP molecules and isolated CMV-specific HLA-DP–restricted T cells from the memory repertoire of healthy donors. First, K562-expressing HLA-DP1 or HLA-DP5 were transduced with the immunodominant CMV proteins pp65, pp50, and IE1. We performed HLA-DP immunoaffinity chromatography and peptide elution and analyzed the samples by mass spectrometry and identified several peptides derived from pp65 and IE1 in HLA-DP1 and HLA-DP5 samples, respectively (
Fig. 2
A
).

To preferably stimulate T cells from the memory compartment, 20 h after peptide stimulation, T cells were sorted based on activation markers CD137 and CD154, seeded as single cells, and after 2 wk of expansion, T cells were tested against peptide-loaded and pp65/pp50/IE1-transduced K562-HLA-DP cells. These results describe four newly identified CMV T cell epitopes in seropositive healthy donors restricted to HLA-DP1 and HLA-DP5.
Peptide Core Motifs from Identified CMV Epitopes.
Next, to determine the peptide-binding core of the identified CMV epitopes, a peptide library containing 15-mer peptides shifted by one amino acid along the sequence of peptides 1–4 (
Fig. 2
A
) was synthesized. After loading those length variants on K562-HLA-DP cells, amino acids being essential for the minimal peptide core were identified by IFN-γ release of T cell clones (
Fig. 3
). The minimal core of peptide 1 (ATTFLQTMLRKEVNSQ) is FLQTMLRKE (
Fig. 3
A
), of peptide 3 (TPVTKATTFLQTMLRKE) is KATTFLQTM (
Fig. 3
C
), and of peptide 4 (YTSAFVFPTKDVAL) is AFVFPTKDV (
Fig. 3
D
). These results were also confirmed by using shorter (10- and 11-mer) peptides (
SI Appendix

–

After experimentally defining the minimal peptide core, we determined whether peptides 1–4 could most likely be categorized into the forward or reverse cluster. Aligning peptides 1 and 3 to the core motifs of HLA-DP1 and HLA-DP5, respectively, both peptides obviously fit to the forward motif (

Frequencies of Reverse Peptide–Specific T Cells within the Memory Pool of Healthy Donors.
We determined the frequencies of T cells specific for peptides 1–4 in additional healthy donors by stimulating the PBMCs with the single peptides (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S5
). Here, 0.16 to 0.33% peptide-reactive CD4
+
TNF-α
+
IFN-γ
+
cells of total CD4
+
T cells were detected after stimulating with the single peptides. By testing six HLA-DPB1*01:01-positive donors, no clear reactivity was detectable against the forward peptide 1, and one donor showed reactivity against the reverse peptide 2. In 1 out of 6 HLA-DP5
+
donors, reactivity was found against the forward peptide 3, and three donors showed a response against the reverse peptide 4. These results demonstrate that T cell responses against reverse peptides occur at similar frequencies compared with those against forward peptides.
Crystal Structure of Peptide 2–HLA-DP1 Complex.
To investigate the orientation adopted by peptide 2 (CMV pp65
(142–158)
) in the HLA-DP1 antigen-binding cleft, we determined the crystal structure of HLA-DP1 in complex with this peptide at a resolution of 2.3 Å, with an unambiguous electron density map (
Fig. 5
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S6 and Table S3
). With respect to canonical HLA–peptide binding, the peptide 2–HLA-DP1 complex revealed an inverted peptide alignment, with the C- to N-terminus of the peptide spanning through the major histocompatibility complex (MHC)-binding groove and occupying the P1, P6, and P9 binding pockets (conventional labeling for MHC class II) (
Fig. 5
A
and
B
). The P1 pocket was occupied by the anchor residue lysine (P1-K), toward the C-terminus of peptide 2, forming a salt bridge with the negatively charged HLA-DP1 D84β (
Fig. 5
C
). The P6 binding pocket was occupied by isoleucine (P6-I) of peptide 2 and formed multiple contacts with the HLA-DP1 α- (N62α, I65α, and L66α) and β-chains (Q13β, E26β, Y28β, and K69β) (
Fig. 5
D
). Aspartic acid (P9-D) of peptide 2 served as the final anchor residue within the P9 pocket (
Fig. 5
E
). The occupancy of the P1, P6, and P9 binding pockets of the peptide 2 structure concurs with the peptide-binding motif we determined for HLA-DP1 (
Fig. 1
).

The HLA-DP1 α- and β-chain residues are colored in cyan and blue, respectively, while HLA-DP5 residues are colored in dark gray. Electrostatic surface potential of (

We additionally compared our structure of the inverted peptide 2 bound to HLA-DP1 with the closest structure solved to date, that of HLA-DP5 presenting the Cryj1 peptide in a canonical N- to C-terminus register (
13
). The two structures revealed surprisingly highly similar features with respect to the interactions of anchor residues in the P1 and P6 binding pockets (
Fig. 5
F
). Moreover, structural superposition of both inverted and canonical complexes revealed a highly conserved main chain hydrogen bonding pattern, with the reverse peptide 2 being shifted a distance of ~1.1 Å in the antigen-binding groove relative to the Cryj1 peptide in HLA-DP5 (
Fig. 5
G
). The electrostatic surface potential of HLA-DP1 and HLA-DP5 complexes further illustrates that the critical features determining the differences in the peptide register between HLA-DP1 and HLA-DP5 are located in the P9 pocket, which is positively charged in HLA-DP1 compared with neutral in HLA-DP5 (
Fig. 5
H
and
I
).
In conclusion, our data clearly demonstrate that peptide 2 binds in a C- to N-terminal orientation within HLA-DP1.
Discussion
For decades, the general understanding has been that peptides bind from the N to C terminus within the HLA groove. It was previously shown that the CLIP can bind in a bidirectional manner in HLA-DR1 (
4
,
14
). However, the CLIP functions as a placeholder within HLA class II molecules, and the sequence of CLIP has a pseudosymmetry, which both are special circumstances allowing different binding modes. It remained unclear whether naturally occurring peptides could bind to other HLA class II allotypes with a reverse peptide–binding orientation. Moreover, it was unknown if human T cells can recognize such peptides. Here, we show that a broad range of HLA-DP allotypes present peptides with a reverse motif and that virus-specific human T cells from the memory repertoire of different donors recognize reverse peptides. Importantly, we finally prove reverse peptide binding by crystal structures of an HLA-DP1–peptide complex.
We observed reverse motifs in 9 out of 14 analyzed HLA-DP allotypes, demonstrating that reverse peptide binding is a common circumstance rather than a rare phenomenon. These nine HLA-DP alleles showing a reverse motif are expressed in 16% of humans in the worldwide population, with strong regional differences (
15
). For example, we discovered a reverse motif in HLA-DP5, which is with 36 to 44% the most frequent HLA-DPB1 allele in the Indonesian and Japanese population (
16
), whereas in the European population, it is expressed in about 2% (
15
). This implies an important role for these HLA alleles in the control of certain pathogens in those regions.
We did not find a reverse motif in HLA-DPB1*02:01, *03:01, *04:01, *04:02, and *06:01. These five HLA-DPB1 alleles are most often linked with HLA-DPA1*01:03 (
17
). In sharp contrast, all HLA-DPB1 alleles where we identified a reverse motif are associated with HLA-DPA1*02:01 or *02:02. This suggests an influence of the HLA-DP α-chain on the reverse motif, and further studies are required to reveal the impact of the HLA-DP α-chain. In addition, a common feature of HLA-DP molecules showing a reverse motif is a lysine (K) at P1, in contrast to HLA-DPB1*02:01, 04:01, and 04:02 with dominant hydrophobic amino acids leucine (L) and phenylalanine (F) or HLA-DPB1*03:01 and 06:01 with an arginine (R). To date, only two HLA-DP crystal structures were available (HLA-DPB1*02:01 and *05:01) (
13
,
18
). We now revealed the structure of peptide 2–HLA-DP1 complex and demonstrate highly similar features regarding the interactions of anchor residues in the P1 and P6 binding pockets of HLA-DP1 and HLA-DP5. P1 is negatively charged, mainly because of two amino acids from the HLA molecule (Q31α and D84β), and is especially suitable for positively charged amino acids, like arginine (R) or lysine (K), which is reflected by the peptide motif. The most influential amino acids of P9 of HLA-DPB1*01:01 are Y9β, Y35β, A36β, and A55β, which are in this combination only shared by HLA-DPB1*11:01 and *13:01 in the dataset we analyzed (
5
,
19
,
20
). Accordingly, all three HLA alleles share unique preferences compared with other HLA-DP alleles for negatively charged amino acids like aspartic acid (D) and glutamic acid (E) at this position and form a positively charged P9. In conclusion, reverse binding is from a biochemical point of view the only possible binding mode as we show by the HLA–peptide structure.
This finding has a significant impact since reverse binding modes will tremendously increase the possibilities of peptide antigens and therefore will broaden our T cell repertoire. We detected reverse peptide–reactive T cells more often in healthy donors and also at the same frequencies compared with forward peptides, most notably showing that reverse peptides are as immunogenic as forward peptides. Our data do not indicate that TCRs from T cell clones recognizing reverse peptides differ from TCRs recognizing forward peptides. This is suggested by a similar level of recognition of endogenously processed antigen and peptide-loaded cells. In addition, the amino acid sequences of the TCRs do not imply obvious differences between TCRs recognizing forward or reverse binding peptides. However, TCR binding modes might be different, which is an interesting aspect for future studies.
Our finding is of relevance since epitope prediction algorithms have emerged as a powerful tool in the identification of virus- and tumor-specific T cell responses (
21
,
22
). However, current algorithms thus far only consider peptides with an N- to C-terminal binding in their prediction models (
7
). Thus, considering also peptides with a reverse motif would increase the number of potential epitopes, which otherwise would have been missed. Future studies have to determine whether peptides with a reverse motif also commonly exist in other HLA class I and class II alleles. However, reverse peptides might be less likely to be found in HLA class I molecules because of the closed peptide-binding groove. In addition, using MoDec, we do not have evidence that reverse binding occurs in a limited dataset of HLA-DR or HLA-DQ, pointing to a unique feature of HLA-DP.
In summary, our results demonstrate that peptides frequently bind in a reverse orientation to HLA-DP, and virus-specific T cells from healthy individuals can recognize those peptides. These findings fundamentally change our understanding of how peptides are bound to HLA molecules, which further highly impacts the discovery of T cell epitopes against pathogens and cancer cells.
Methods
Cell Lines and Primary Material.
K562 cells lacking HLA class I and class II surface expression were cultured in Iscove’s modified Dulbecco’s medium (IMDM) (Lonza, Switzerland) with 10% fetal bovine serum (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), 200 mM L-glutamine (Lonza), and 10,000 U/ml penicillin/streptomycin (Lonza). Cells were transduced with HLA-DP using the pLZRS vector encoding for HLA-DPA1-T2A-DPB1-IRES-ΔNGFR or HLA-DPA1-IRES-GFP and HLA-DPB1-IRES-ΔNGFR. Purity of HLA-DP–expressing cells was verified by flow cytometry. T cells isolated from healthy donors were cultured in T cell medium consisting of IMDM with 5% fetal bovine serum, 5% human serum, 200 mM L-glutamine, 10,000 U/ml penicillin/streptomycin, and IL-2 (Novartis, Switzerland) as indicated below. Human samples were deidentified prior to use and the study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Leiden University Medical Centre.
HLA-DP Immunoaffinity Chromatography and Mass Spectrometry.
HLA-DP immunoaffinity chromatography was performed as recently described (
5
). Briefly, Protein A Sepharose bead (GE Healthcare)–purified B7/21 antibody was used to generate a 2.5 mg/ml immunoaffinity column. Approximately 1 × 10
8
cells/ml were lysed 2 h at 4°C using 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8), 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, 0.5% Zwittergent
®
3–12 detergent (Merck, Germany), and complete™ protease inhibitor cocktail (Merck). After centrifugation (13,640 g, 30 min, 4°C), supernatant was precleared using CL4B beads (GE Healthcare) and transferred to the immunoaffinity column. Elution from bound peptide–HLA-DP complexes was performed with 10% acetic acid. Subsequently, size filtration through a 10-kDa membrane (Merck) and freeze-drying were carried out. Mass spectrometry was performed as described elsewhere (
5
).
Peptide Data Analysis.
Peptide motifs were aligned and clustered with the previously published algorithm MoDec using default settings (
7
), except for the K562 dataset where the peptide input length was set to nine amino acids since K562 lack HLA class I expression. HLA-DP peptide elution datasets from EBV-LCL and K562 transduced were published earlier (
5
,
23
) and reanalyzed with MoDec. Datasets for HLA-DR and HLA-DQ were obtained from studies published by others (
9
,
10
) and were analyzed with MoDec.
Isolation of CMV-Specific T Cell Clones.
PBMCs from CMV-seropositive healthy donors were stimulated with 1 µM peptide mix (dependent on the HLA type of the donor;
Fig. 2
A
) at a concentration of 2 × 10
7
cells/ml in T cell medium supplemented with 20 U/ml IL-2 for 20 h. Peptides were synthesized in-house by our peptide synthesis facility. Cells were harvested and stained with the following fluorochrome-labeled monoclonal antibodies: anti-human CD3 (UCHT1) Alexa Fluor 700, CD4 (RPA-T4) FITC, and CD137 (4B4-1) APC (all from BD Biosciences, Germany) and CD154 (TRAP-1) PE (Beckman Coulter, USA). After sorting with BD FACSAria™, T cells were plated and expanded in single cells in 384-well plates together with 35-Gy irradiated allogeneic PBMCs (25,000 per well) in T cell medium supplemented with 200 U/ml IL-2 and 0.8 µg/ml phytohemagglutinin (PHA; Thermo Fisher Scientific). Seven days later, T cells were restimulated with 50,000 irradiated allogeneic PBMCs per well. Between days 3 and 5 after restimulation, growing T cell clones were transferred into 96-well plates. Subsequently, T cells were tested for peptide recognition and endogenously processed antigen against K562 cells as described below. Clonality of the T cell clones was analyzed by staining the variable domain from the T cell receptor β-chain with the Beta Mark TCR Vbeta Repertoire Kit (Beckman Coulter).
IFN-γ ELISA.
T cell clones were tested for IFN-γ production 10–14 d after restimulation. About 2,000 T cell clones were incubated overnight with 10,000 target cells in 384-well plates in 60 µl T cell medium supplemented with 20 U/ml IL-2. K562 transduced with either HLA-DPA1*02:01/DPB1*01:01 (K562-HLA-DP1) or HLA-DPA1*02:02/DPB1*05:01 (K562-HLA-DP5) were loaded with peptide as indicated for 1 h at 37°C and washed before coincubation with T cells. To test recognition of endogenously processed antigen, K562-DP1 or K562-DP5 cells transduced with pp65, IE1, and pp50 were used as target cells. Technical replicates of supernatants were analyzed for IFN-γ secretion using the Human IFN-γ ELISA Set (Diaclone, France) according to manufacturer’s instructions.
Ten-Day T Cell Stimulation Assay.
PBMCs from healthy CMV-seropositive donors that express HLA-DPB1*01:01 and/or HLA-DPB1*05:01 were incubated (37°C + 5% CO
2
) with 1 µg/mL peptide in IMDM (Lonza) with 10% fetal bovine serum (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 200 mM L-glutamine (Lonza), and 10,000 U/ml penicillin/streptomycin (Lonza). Half of medium was refreshed daily, and after 10 d of culturing, the cells were restimulated with the same peptide. After 1-h incubation, 5 µg/mL Brefeldin A (Sigma-Aldrich) was added and incubated for an additional 15 h. The reaction was stopped by washing in PBS, followed by Zombie-red staining (BioLegend). After incubation for 20 min at room temperature (RT), cells were fixated and permeabilized using the eBioscience Foxp3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer Set (Invitrogen), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Cells were incubated for 30 min at RT with an antibody mix containing Brilliant Violet Staining Buffer Plus (BD Biosciences), CD3-PE-Texas Red (7D6; Invitrogen), CD8-APC-H7 (SK1; BD Biosciences), CD4-BV510 (SK3; BD Biosciences), IFNγ-BV711 (B27; BD Biosciences), and TNFα-BV421 (Mab11; BD Biosciences). After incubation, cells were washed and resuspended in PBS containing 400 mg albumin for measurement on a 3-laser Aurora (Cytek Biosciences). Data were analyzed using OMIQ (
https://www.omiq.ai/
).
HLA-DP1-CLIP Expression and Purification.
The gene encoding the GP67 signal sequence and extracellular domains of the HLA-DP1 α- and β-chains (HLA-DPA1*02:01 and HLA-DPB1*01:01) were cloned into the pZIP3 bidirectional baculovirus expression vector (
24
). A DNA sequence encoding the Strep-TagII CLIP sequence (Strep-TagII-CLIP: WSHPQFEKGAPVSKMRMATPLLMQA) was inserted upstream of the gene encoding the HLA-DPB1 extracellular domain, connected by a flexible Factor Xa (FXa) cleavable linker (FXa recognition sequence underlined; GSGGS
IEGR
GSGSG) at the N terminus of the HLA-DPB1 gene. The C terminus of the construct encoded a Fos/Jun leucine zipper for the α- and β-chains, respectively, with both connected via 3C protease cleavage sites (LEVLFQGP) in between. The C terminus of the β-chain encoded a BirA biotinylation recognition site (GLNDIFEAQKIEWHE), and a polyhistidine-tag for purification of the expressed protein via immobilized metal affinity chromatography (IMAC). The DP1-CLIP molecule was expressed in High Five insect cells (Trichoplusia ni BTI-TN-5B1-4 cells; Thermo Fisher Scientific) using the Bac-to-Bac baculovirus system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to generate recombinant virus for protein expression. The High Five insect cells were infected with recombinant virus and incubated for 72 h at 27°C in shaking cultures (120 RPM). Culture supernatant containing the protein was separated from cells by centrifugation, followed by concentration and diafiltration using a Cogent M1 tangential flow filtration apparatus (Merck) with proteins then purified using a combination of IMAC (Nickel Sepharose 6 Fast Flow; Cytiva), size exclusion (Superdex 200, 16/600; Cytiva), and anion exchange (HiTrap Q HP column; Cytiva) chromatography.
Peptide Loading of HLA-DP1.
A 17-mer pp65 peptide (denoted as peptide 2) was synthesized by GL Biochem (China). The integrity of the peptides was verified by reverse-phase HPLC and mass spectrometry. HLA-DP1 was digested with Factor Xa (New England BioLabs, MA, USA) in the presence of 2 mM CaCl
2
to cleave the covalently linked Strep-TagII-CLIP peptide (WSHPQFEKGAPVSKMRMATPLLMQAGSGGSIEGRGSGSG). The Strep-TagII-CLIP peptide in HLA-DP1 was exchanged with the pp65
142–158
peptide using a 20-fold molar excess of peptide to HLA-DP1 in a buffer comprising 50 mM trisodium citrate pH 5.4 and 5 mM EDTA at 37°C for 24–72 h in the presence of HLA-DM (1:5 molar ratio HLA-DM:HLA-DP1). Peptide 2–loaded HLA-DP1 was separated from unloaded HLA-DP1-Strep-TagII-CLIP using Strep-Tactin Sepharose (IBA, Gottingen, Germany). Peptide 2–HLA-DP1 was subjected to 3C protease cleavage in order to remove the Fos/Jun leucine zippers and further purified using anion exchange (HiTrap Q HP column; Cytiva) chromatography. Final purified proteins were pooled and concentrated to 10 mg/ml.
Crystallization, Data Collection, and Processing.
Crystallization of the peptide 2–HLA-DP1 complex was carried out using the broad screen sitting-drop vapor-diffusion method (Monash Molecular Crystallisation Facility, Monash University, Clayton, Australia). Crystal hits were obtained in solution containing 0.1 M sodium cacodylate pH 5.5 and 20 to 25% PEG4000. Crystals were cryoprotected in 20% glycerol prior to flash freezing in liquid N
2
. Data were collected at the microfocus beamline (MX2) of the Australian Synchrotron (Victoria, Australia) and autoprocessed using program XDS (
25
) at the Australian Synchrotron.
Structure Determination, Refinement, and Validation.
Complex structures were solved by molecular replacement in PHASER (
26
), CCP4 (
27
) suite using a separate search model of HLA-DP5 (PDB ID: 3WEX). Iterative rounds of model building in Coot and restrained refinement using REFMAC (CCP4 suite) (
27
) and PhenixRefine (PHENIX) (
28
) were carried out. The crystal structures were validated using the Protein Data Bank (PDB) structure validation server. Data processing and refinement statistics are summarized in
SI Appendix
, Table S1
. The Ramachandran statistic of final models revealed 99.5% of residues in favored regions, with no outlier residues. All structural figures were generated by PyMOL (
http://www.pymol.org/
).
Accession Number.
The X-ray crystal structure of peptide 2–HLA-DP1 was deposited in the PDB with the accession code 7T6I.
